stem: The student wants to present the aim of Ferreira's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In a whistled language, speakers replace spoken syllables with whistled pitches so that messages carry across long distances.
• Linguist Tomas Ferreira asked whether people who had never heard a whistled language could still recognize whistled vowels.
• He played 120 recordings of whistled vowels to 40 French speakers with no prior exposure to whistled speech.
• The listeners identified the vowels correctly 63% of the time, well above chance.
• Ferreira concluded that whistled vowels preserve acoustic cues that any listener can use.
choices: Ferreira found that listeners with no exposure to whistled speech identified whistled vowels correctly 63% of the time.
Ferreira sought to determine whether listeners unfamiliar with whistled languages could still recognize whistled vowels.
In Ferreira's study, 40 French speakers with no prior exposure to whistled speech heard 120 whistled vowels.
Ferreira sought to show that any human language could be whistled and understood by listeners anywhere.
explanation: The goal asks for the aim, which is the question the study set out to answer. You want a choice built on the note that begins 'asked whether.' Choice B states that question: could listeners who had never heard a whistled language still recognize whistled vowels? It doesn't wander into the method or the result.

A.why: You picked the study's result instead of its aim. 'Found' reports what happened after the study was run. The goal asks what Ferreira set out to learn.

C.why: You picked a description of the method, meaning who listened to what. It explains how the study was done but never says what question it was meant to answer.

D.why: 'Sought to' makes this sound like an aim, but the aim it names isn't in the notes. Ferreira asked about recognizing vowels, not whether every language could be whistled and understood everywhere.

stem: The student wants to present Okafor's study and its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Beavers build dams that slow streams and create ponds.
• During a 2021 drought, ecologist Hana Okafor studied 18 Montana streams, half with beaver dams and half without.
• She used satellite imagery to measure how far green vegetation extended from each stream.
• Along dammed streams, the band of green vegetation was 40% wider than along undammed streams.
• Okafor concluded that beaver dams can help streamside habitats withstand drought.
choices: During a 2021 drought, Okafor used satellite imagery to examine vegetation along 18 Montana streams, half of them dammed.
Beaver dams, which slow streams and create ponds, can help streamside habitats withstand periods of drought.
Comparing 18 Montana streams during a 2021 drought, Okafor found that green vegetation extended 40% wider along dammed streams.
Okafor found that beaver dams keep streamside vegetation green during every drought, in Montana and elsewhere.
explanation: 'Study and its findings' asks for two things: the study and what it found. Choice C names the study (Okafor comparing 18 Montana streams during a 2021 drought) and gives its result (vegetation extended 40% wider along dammed streams). No other choice supplies both halves accurately.

A.why: You stopped halfway. This describes the study's setup and method, but it never says what Okafor found, so the 'findings' half of the goal is missing.

B.why: This gives the general conclusion but never mentions Okafor's study or its measured result. The goal asks you to present the study itself, not just the lesson drawn from it.

D.why: This names a finding, but it stretches one drought in 18 Montana streams into a claim about every drought everywhere. The notes support nothing that broad.

stem: The student wants to present the conclusion that Raman's team reached. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Self-healing concrete contains bacterial spores that produce limestone when water seeps into cracks.
• Engineers led by Priya Raman wanted to know whether such concrete could repair itself in cold climates.
• They cast 60 test beams, cracked them, and stored them at 4°C for 90 days.
• Cracks narrower than 0.4 mm sealed completely; wider cracks sealed only partly.
• The team concluded that the concrete is suitable for cold-climate use only where cracks are expected to stay small.
choices: In Raman's study, cracks narrower than 0.4 mm sealed completely at 4°C, while wider cracks sealed only partly.
Raman's team concluded that self-healing concrete can fully seal cracks of any width, even in cold climates.
Raman's team wanted to know whether concrete containing bacterial spores could repair itself in cold climates.
Raman's team concluded that self-healing concrete suits cold climates only where cracks are expected to stay small.
explanation: A conclusion is the interpretation the researchers drew from their results, and the last note gives it. Choice D restates it: the concrete is suitable for cold climates only where cracks will stay small.

A.why: This is the finding, the raw result about crack widths. The conclusion is what the team decided those results mean for real-world use, and that isn't stated here.

B.why: It uses the word 'concluded,' but it reverses the notes. Wider cracks sealed only partly, so the team did not conclude that cracks of any width would seal.

C.why: This is the study's aim, the question it began with. The goal asks where the study ended up, not where it started.

stem: The student wants to present the recommendation that came out of Varga's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Flu vaccines are usually given at whatever time of day a clinic has an opening.
• Immunologist Lena Varga's team asked whether the time of vaccination affects antibody response in adults over 65.
• They randomly assigned 400 older adults to morning (9–11 a.m.) or afternoon (3–5 p.m.) vaccination.
• One month later, the morning group's antibody levels were about 20% higher.
• The team recommended that clinics schedule older patients' flu shots in the morning when possible.
choices: Varga's team recommended that clinics, when possible, give older patients their flu shots in the morning.
A month after vaccination, older adults who received morning flu shots had antibody levels about 20% higher.
Varga's team recommended that clinics give patients of every age their flu shots only in the morning.
Varga's team asked whether the time of day of a flu shot affects antibody response in adults over 65.
explanation: A recommendation is advice about what someone should do. The final note gives the team's advice, and choice A states it accurately: when possible, clinics should schedule older patients' flu shots in the morning.

B.why: This is the finding that led to the recommendation, not the recommendation itself. It reports antibody levels but tells clinics nothing about what to do.

C.why: This is framed as a recommendation, but the study covered only adults over 65, and the team said 'when possible.' Extending it to every age and to 'only' in the morning goes beyond what the team advised.

D.why: This is the research question from the start of the study. It says what the team wondered about, not what they advised clinics to do.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the aim of Morales's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Parking minimums require new buildings to include a set number of parking spaces.
• Critics of eliminating these rules warn that developers would stop building parking altogether.
• Urban planner Diego Morales set out to learn how much parking developers actually build once minimums are lifted.
• He compared 310 housing projects in one midsize US city, approved before and after it dropped its minimums in 2017.
• Projects approved after 2017 included 41% fewer spaces on average, but 88% still included some parking.
choices: Critics warn that if cities eliminate parking minimums, developers will stop building parking for new housing altogether.
After the city dropped its parking minimums in 2017, new projects had 41% fewer spaces, though 88% still had some parking.
Morales set out to learn how much parking developers actually build once cities stop requiring a minimum number of spaces.
Morales set out to prove that critics were wrong to warn that developers would stop building parking altogether.
explanation: The aim is what the researcher set out to learn. Choice C is built on the note that says 'set out to learn' and puts that purpose at the center: how much parking developers build once the requirement is gone.

A.why: This is the background debate that makes the study matter. It states the critics' worry, but it never mentions Morales or what his study was trying to find out.

B.why: This reports the study's results. They answer Morales's question, but the goal asks you to emphasize the question itself, not the answer.

D.why: The 'set out to' framing sounds like an aim, but the notes never say Morales was trying to prove the critics wrong. He wanted to measure what developers do, and this choice gives him a motive the notes don't support.

stem: The student wants to describe the method Solberg used in her research. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Written records rarely specify the tempos at which 18th-century dance music was played.
• Musicologist Ingrid Solberg wanted to estimate those tempos from barrel organs, mechanical instruments whose pinned barrels preserve performances.
• She measured pin spacing and rotation speed on 26 barrel organs built between 1740 and 1790.
• Minuets on the organs ran about 30% faster than modern performers typically play them.
• Solberg concluded that modern performances of minuets may be too slow.
choices: Solberg found that 18th-century minuets ran about 30% faster than modern performers typically play them.
Solberg measured the pin spacing and rotation speed of 26 barrel organs built between 1740 and 1790.
Solberg wanted to estimate 18th-century dance tempos from barrel organs, whose pinned barrels preserve performances.
Solberg examined every surviving 18th-century barrel organ to determine how fast all dance music was played.
explanation: A method is what the researcher physically did to get data. Choice B gives those steps: Solberg measured pin spacing and rotation speed on 26 barrel organs from 1740 to 1790.

A.why: This is the result the method produced. It tells you what Solberg discovered, not how she went about discovering it.

C.why: This one is close because it mentions barrel organs, but it states her aim ('wanted to estimate'). It says what she hoped to do with the organs, not the measurements she actually took.

D.why: Solberg studied 26 organs from a 50-year span, not every surviving one, and she estimated tempos for minuets, not for all dance music. This inflates both the sample and the scope.

stem: The student wants to present Mensah's study and its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The human gut contains trillions of bacteria, and greater diversity among them is linked to better health.
• Nutrition scientist Kofi Mensah's team asked whether eating fermented foods would increase gut bacterial diversity.
• For 10 weeks, 36 healthy adults ate six servings a day of fermented foods such as yogurt, kimchi, and kefir.
• Stool samples showed that participants' gut bacterial diversity rose steadily over the 10 weeks.
• Markers of inflammation fell in the participants whose diversity rose the most.
choices: Mensah's team had 36 healthy adults eat six daily servings of fermented foods for 10 weeks to test whether gut diversity would rise.
Eating fermented foods such as yogurt, kimchi, and kefir raises the diversity of gut bacteria and lowers inflammation in adults.
Mensah's team found that fermented foods lowered markers of inflammation in all 36 adults who ate six servings a day.
After 36 adults ate six daily servings of fermented foods for 10 weeks, Mensah's team found that their gut diversity had risen.
explanation: The goal needs both the study and what it found. Choice D gives the study (36 adults, six daily servings of fermented foods, 10 weeks) and its main result (gut bacterial diversity rose).

A.why: This is the tempting half-answer. It covers the method and the aim in detail, but 'to test whether' leaves the outcome unknown, so the findings are never presented.

B.why: This states a general health claim but never mentions Mensah's study. The goal asks you to present the research, not just a takeaway from it.

C.why: Inflammation markers fell only in the participants whose diversity rose the most, not in all 36. This choice misreports the finding.

stem: The student wants to present the conclusion that Adeyemi's team reached. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hailstones grow as updrafts carry them repeatedly above the freezing level of a storm.
• Forecasters have long struggled to predict hailstone size from radar data.
• Meteorologist Ruth Adeyemi's team compared radar-measured updraft width with reported hail size for 214 Great Plains storms.
• Storms with updrafts wider than 10 km produced hail larger than 5 cm far more often than narrower storms did.
• The team concluded that hail forecasts should account for updraft width, not just updraft speed.
choices: Storms with updrafts wider than 10 km produced hail larger than 5 cm far more often than storms with narrower updrafts.
Adeyemi's team compared radar-measured updraft width with reported hail size for 214 storms across the Great Plains.
Adeyemi's team concluded that forecasters predicting hail size should account for updraft width, not just updraft speed.
Adeyemi's team concluded that updraft width alone determines how large hailstones will grow in any storm.
explanation: A conclusion is what the researchers decided their results mean. Choice C restates the team's conclusion from the last note: hail forecasts should factor in updraft width as well as speed.

A.why: This is the finding, the pattern in the storm data. The conclusion is the lesson the team drew from that pattern for forecasting, and this choice leaves it out.

B.why: This describes the method, meaning what the team compared and for how many storms. It says nothing about what they concluded.

D.why: The team said width should be considered along with speed. Saying width 'alone determines' hail size in 'any storm' turns that into a much stronger claim than the evidence supports.

stem: The student wants to present the study's conclusion. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• Lake-effect snow forms when cold air moves across a lake whose open water is warmer than the air.
• Forecasters have long debated whether shrinking winter ice cover on the Great Lakes would increase lake-effect snowfall.
• In 2023, atmospheric scientist Ines Kovač and her team compared ice-cover records with snowfall totals from 41 weather stations downwind of Lake Erie.
• The team examined every winter from 1975 to 2020.
• Winters with less than 20% ice cover by mid-January brought, on average, 34% more lake-effect snow to the stations than icier winters did.
• Kovač concluded that declining ice cover will likely make heavy lake-effect snow events more frequent downwind of Lake Erie in the coming decades.
choices: Comparing ice-cover records with snowfall totals from 41 stations downwind of Lake Erie, Kovač's team examined every winter from 1975 to 2020.
Kovač's team found that winters with under 20% ice cover by mid-January brought about 34% more lake-effect snow than icier winters did.
Based on her team's study, Kovač concluded that shrinking ice cover will likely make heavy lake-effect snow more frequent downwind of Lake Erie.
Based on her team's study, Kovač concluded that shrinking ice cover has already doubled heavy lake-effect snow events throughout the Great Lakes.
explanation: The goal asks for the study's conclusion, which is the interpretation the researcher drew from the results, not the results themselves. The last note gives that conclusion: declining ice will likely make heavy lake-effect snow more frequent downwind of Lake Erie. Choice C presents exactly that claim and keeps the note's hedge ('will likely') and its limited scope (downwind of Lake Erie).

A.why: You chose the study's method. This choice explains how the team gathered its data (the records, the 41 stations, the 45 winters), but the goal asks for what Kovač concluded, and this choice never gets to that.

B.why: This is the trap for this kind of question. You picked the study's finding, the 34% statistic, because a result can look like a conclusion. The goal names the conclusion, though, and that is Kovač's prediction about future snow events. This choice reports what the data showed and leaves out what she concluded from it.

D.why: This choice starts the right way, with 'Kovač concluded,' but it changes what she concluded. The notes give a cautious prediction about the future for the area downwind of Lake Erie. This choice claims the snow events have already doubled across all the Great Lakes, and no note supports that number, that timing, or that wider region.

stem: The student wants to present the conclusion of Ferrante's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Heavy elements such as iron and magnesium should sink out of view in a white dwarf's atmosphere within days.
• Yet some white dwarfs show these elements in their atmospheres.
• Astronomer Lucia Ferrante wanted to know whether debris from destroyed planets was replenishing them.
• Her team measured the ratios of heavy elements in the atmospheres of 40 such stars.
• The ratios closely matched those of rocky bodies such as Earth's crust.
• Ferrante concluded that these stars are actively pulling in material from shattered rocky planets.
choices: Ferrante's team measured the ratios of heavy elements in 40 white dwarf atmospheres to test whether debris from destroyed planets was replenishing them.
Heavy elements in some white dwarf atmospheres should sink out of view within days, which led Ferrante to ask how they were being replenished.
The element ratios that Ferrante's team measured in 40 white dwarf atmospheres closely matched those of rocky bodies such as Earth's crust.
Based on element ratios in 40 white dwarf atmospheres, Ferrante concluded that these stars are actively pulling in material from shattered rocky planets.
explanation: The goal asks for the conclusion, so you need the stage where the researcher says what the evidence means. Choice D uses the word 'concluded' and states Ferrante's interpretation: the stars are pulling in material from shattered rocky planets. It names the evidence only briefly, as the basis for that conclusion.

A.why: You picked the method and the aim. This tells you what the team measured and why, but not what Ferrante concluded. It describes the wrong stage of the study.

B.why: You picked the background puzzle that started the study. The goal asks where the study ended up, and this choice stops before any result or conclusion.

C.why: This is the finding, not the conclusion. The matching ratios are the evidence. The conclusion is what Ferrante decided that evidence means, and this choice never says it. It's the closest near-miss, so check whether a choice reports data or interprets it.

stem: The student wants to emphasize the aim of Okafor's study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Beaver dams create ponds that slow the flow of streams.
• In drought years, many streams in the western United States dry up by late summer.
• Hydrologist Tomas Okafor wondered whether beaver ponds help streams keep flowing through drought.
• During a drought year, he compared late-summer flow in 12 Idaho streams with beaver dams and 12 nearby streams without them.
• Streams with dams kept flowing an average of 23 days longer.
• Okafor suggested that land managers reintroduce beavers to drought-prone watersheds.
choices: Okafor found that Idaho streams with beaver dams kept flowing through a late-summer drought an average of 23 days longer than streams without them.
Okafor set out to learn whether the ponds that beaver dams create can help streams keep flowing through the dry late summers of drought years.
During a drought year, Okafor compared late-summer flow in 12 Idaho streams that had beaver dams and in 12 nearby streams that had none.
Okafor suggested that land managers in drought-prone western watersheds consider reintroducing beavers as a way to keep streams flowing longer.
explanation: An aim is the question a study sets out to answer. Choice B is built around that stage: 'set out to learn whether' introduces the question of whether beaver ponds keep streams flowing through drought. It doesn't report a result.

A.why: You picked the result instead of the aim. This is the subtype's main trap: it covers the same topic as the aim, but it says what Okafor found, not what he set out to find.

C.why: This is the method. It tells you how Okafor ran the comparison, but not the question the comparison was meant to answer.

D.why: This is the recommendation that came after the study. Advice to land managers is the last stage of the research story, not the first.

stem: The student wants to present Varga's study and its findings. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
stimulus:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Eighteenth-century composers marked tempos with words like "allegro" rather than precise speeds.
• Musical clocks of the period played tunes from pinned barrels that fixed each tune's speed.
• Musicologist Ines Varga measured the tempos pinned into 60 musical clocks built in Vienna between 1770 and 1800.
• Pieces marked "allegro" played at an average of 132 beats per minute.
• That is about 15 percent faster than in most modern recordings of the same pieces.
• Varga argues that modern performers may be playing these works too slowly.
choices: Measuring the tempos pinned into 60 musical clocks built in Vienna, Varga found that "allegro" pieces played about 15 percent faster than in modern recordings.
Pieces marked "allegro" in late-eighteenth-century Vienna played at about 132 beats per minute, roughly 15 percent faster than in most modern recordings.
Varga measured the tempos pinned into the barrels of 60 musical clocks built in Vienna between 1770 and 1800, a period when tempo words were imprecise.
Because tempo markings like "allegro" gave no precise speed, Varga argues that modern performers may be playing these Viennese works too slowly.
explanation: The goal names two things, the study and its findings, so the right choice has to include both. Choice A names the study (Varga measured the tempos in 60 Viennese musical clocks) and reports the result (allegro pieces played about 15 percent faster than modern recordings).

B.why: You picked a choice with the findings but no study. It never says who measured what or how. This is the subtype's 'only one of the two' trap, so check that the choice also names the research.

C.why: This one has the study but no findings. It describes what Varga measured and leaves out what the measurements showed, which is the other half of the goal.

D.why: You picked Varga's argument, which is neither the study nor its findings. It also misplaces her reasoning: her argument rests on the clock measurements, not just on the vagueness of tempo words.
